**Cascading Style Sheets** (**CSS**) is a [style sheet language](mw:File/Thumb "button") used for specifying the [presentation](mw:File/Thumb "button") and styling of a document written in a [markup language](mw:File/Thumb "button"), such as [HTML](mw:File/Thumb "button") or [XML](mw:File/Thumb "button") (including XML dialects such as [SVG](mw:File/Thumb "button"), [MathML](mw:File/Thumb "button"), or [XHTML](mw:File/Thumb
"button")).[[2]](mw:File/Thumb "button") CSS is a cornerstone technology of the
[World Wide Web](mw:File/Thumb "button"), alongside HTML and [JavaScript](mw:File/Thumb
"button").[[3]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

CSS is designed to enable the [separation of content and presentation](mw:File/Thumb "button"), including [layout](mw:File/Thumb "button"), [colors](mw:File/Thumb "button"), and [fonts](mw:File/Thumb
"button").[[4]](mw:File/Thumb "button") This separation can improve content [accessibility](mw:File/Thumb "button"), since the content can be written without concern for its presentation; provide more flexibility and control in the specification of presentation characteristics; enable multiple [web pages](mw:File/Thumb "button") to share formatting by specifying the relevant CSS in a separate .css file, which reduces complexity and repetition in the structural content; and enable the .css file to be [cached](mw:File/Thumb "button") to improve the page load speed between the pages that share the file and its formatting.

Separation of formatting and content also makes it feasible to present the same markup
page in different styles for different rendering methods, such as on-screen, in print,
by voice (via speech-based browser or [screen reader](mw:File/Thumb "button")), and on [Braille-based](mw:File/Thumb "button") tactile devices. CSS also has rules for alternative formatting if the content is accessed on a [mobile device](mw:File/Thumb
"button").[[5]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

The name *cascading* comes from the specified priority scheme to determine which
declaration applies if more than one declaration of a property match a particular
element. This cascading priority scheme is predictable.

The CSS specifications are maintained by the [World Wide Web Consortium](mw:File/Thumb "button") (W3C). Internet media type ([MIME type](mw:File/Thumb "button")) `text/css`
is registered for use with CSS by RFC 2318 (March 1998). The W3C operates a free
[CSS validation service](mw:File/Thumb "button") for CSS documents.[[6]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

In addition to HTML, other markup languages support the use of CSS including [XHTML](mw:File/Thumb "button"), [plain XML](mw:File/Thumb "button"), [SVG](mw:File/Thumb "button"), and [XUL](mw:File/Thumb "button"). CSS is also used in the [GTK](mw:File/Thumb "button") [widget toolkit](mw:File/Thumb "button").


## Syntax
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
CSS has a simple [syntax](mw:File/Thumb "button") and uses a number of English keywords to specify the names of various style properties.


### Style sheet
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]

Main article: [Style sheet (web development)](mw:File/Thumb "button")
A style sheet consists of a list of *rules*. Each rule or rule-set consists of one
or more *[selectors](mw:File/Thumb "button")*, and a *[declaration block](mw:File/Thumb "button")*.


### Selector
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]

"CSS class" redirects here. For element classes that are part of the HTML content
model upon which the CSS class selector syntax depends, see [class attribute (HTML)](mw:File/Thumb "button").
In CSS, *selectors* declare which part of the markup a style applies to by matching
tags and attributes in the markup itself.


#### Selector types
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Selectors may apply to the following:

- all [elements](mw:File/Thumb "button") of a specific type, e.g. the second-level headers [h2](mw:File/Thumb "button")
- elements specified by [attribute](mw:File/Thumb "button"), in particular:- *id*: an identifier unique within the document, denoted in the selector language by a [hash](mw:File/Thumb "button") prefix e.g. `#id`
- *class*: an identifier that can annotate multiple elements in a document, denoted by a [dot](mw:File/Thumb "button") prefix e.g. `.classname` (the phrase "CSS class", although sometimes used, is a misnomer, as element classes—specified with the [HTML class attribute](mw:File/Thumb "button")—is a markup feature that is distinct from browsers' CSS subsystems, and the related W3C/WHATWG standards work on document styles; see [RDF](mw:File/Thumb "button") and [microformats](mw:File/Thumb "button") for the origins of the "class" system of the Web content model)
- elements depending on how they are placed relative to others in the [document tree](mw:File/Thumb "button").

Classes and IDs are case-sensitive, start with letters, and can include alphanumeric
characters, hyphens, and underscores. A class may apply to any number of instances
of any element. An ID may only be applied to a single element.


#### Pseudo-classes
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]

"Pseudo-element" redirects here. For pseudoelement symbols in chemistry, see [Skeletal formula
§ Pseudoelement symbols](mw:File/Thumb "button").
*Pseudo-classes* are used in CSS selectors to permit formatting based on information
that is not contained in the document tree.

One example of a widely used pseudo-class is `:hover`, which identifies content only when
the user "points to" the visible element, usually by holding the mouse cursor over
it. It is appended to a selector as in `a:hover` or `#elementid:hover`.

A pseudo-class classifies document elements, such as `:link` or `:visited`, whereas a *pseudo-element*
makes a selection that may consist of partial elements, such as `::first-line` or `::first-letter`.[[7]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.pygments%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cjquery.tablesorter.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Note the distinction between the double-colon notation used for pseudo-elements and
the single-colon notation used for pseudo-classes.


#### Combinators
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
Multiple simple selectors may be joined using combinators to specify elements by
location, element type, id, class, or any combination thereof.[[8]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
The order of the selectors is important. For example, `div .myClass {color: red;}` applies to all elements
of class myClass that are inside div elements, whereas `.myClass div {color: red;}` applies to all div elements
that are inside elements of class myClass. This is not to be confused with concatenated
identifiers such as `div.myClass {color: red;}` which applies to div elements of class myClass.

### Declaration block
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
A declaration block consists of a pair of braces (`{}`) enclosing a semicolon-separated
list of *declarations*.[[10]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### Declaration
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Each declaration itself consists of a *property*, a colon (`:`), and a *value*. Optional
white-space may be around the declaration block, declarations, colons, and semi-colons
for readability.[[11]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### Properties
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Properties are specified in the CSS standard. Each property has a set of possible
values. Some properties can affect any type of element, and others apply only to
particular groups of elements.[[12]](mw:File/Thumb "button")[[13]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### Values
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Values may be keywords, such as "center" or "inherit", or numerical values, such
as `200px` (200 pixels), `50vw` (50 percent of the viewport width) or 80% (80 percent of the
parent element's width).

Color values can be specified with keywords (e.g. "`red`"), hexadecimal values (e.g.
`#FF0000`, also abbreviated as `#F00`), RGB values on a 0 to 255 scale (e.g. ``rgb(255, 0, 0)``), RGBA values
that specify both color and alpha transparency (e.g. `rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.8)`), or HSL or HSLA values (e.g.
`hsl(0 100% 50%)`, `hsl(0 100% 50% / 0.8)`).[[14]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

Non-zero numeric values representing linear measures must include a length unit,
which is either an alphabetic code or abbreviation, as in `200px` or `50vw`; or a percentage
sign, as in `80%`. Some units – `cm` ([centimetre](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")); `in`
([inch](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")); `mm`
([millimetre](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")); `pc`
([pica](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")); and `pt`
([point](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")) – are
*absolute*, which means that the rendered dimension does not depend upon the structure
of the page; others – `em` ([em](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")); `ex`
([ex](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")) and `px`
([pixel](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url("))[*[clarification needed](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")*] – are *relative*, which means that factors such as the font size of a
parent element can affect the rendered measurement. These eight units were a feature
of CSS 1[[15]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
and retained in all subsequent revisions. The proposed CSS Values and Units Module
Level 3 will, if adopted as a W3C Recommendation, provide seven further length units:
`ch`; `Q`; `rem`; `vh`; `vmax`; `vmin`; and `vw`.[[16]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")


### Use
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
Before CSS, nearly all presentational attributes of HTML documents were contained
within the HTML markup. That is, all font colors, background styles, element alignments,
borders, and sizes had to be explicitly described (often repeatedly) within the HTML.
CSS lets authors move much of that information to another file, the style sheet,
resulting in considerably simpler HTML. And additionally, as more and more devices
are able to access responsive web pages, different screen sizes and layouts begin
to appear. Customizing a website for each device size is costly and increasingly
difficult. The modular nature of CSS means that styles can be reused in different
parts of a site or even across sites, promoting consistency and efficiency.

For example, headings (`h1` elements), sub-headings (`h2`), sub-sub-headings (`h3`), etc.,
are defined structurally using HTML. In print and on the screen, choice of [font](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("), [size](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("), [color](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") and [emphasis](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") for these elements is
*presentational*.

Before CSS, document authors who wanted to assign such [typographic](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") characteristics to, say, all `h2`
headings had to repeat HTML presentational markup for each occurrence of that heading
type. This made documents more complex, larger, and more error-prone and difficult
to maintain. CSS allows the separation of presentation from structure. CSS can define
color, font, text alignment, size, borders, spacing, layout and many other typographic
characteristics, and can do so independently for on-screen and printed views. CSS
also defines non-visual styles, such as reading speed and emphasis for aural text
readers. The [W3C](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") has now [deprecated](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") the use of all presentational HTML
markup.[[17]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

For example, under pre-CSS HTML, a heading element defined with red text would be
written as:

Chapter 1.\\n"}}">

```<h1><font color="red">Chapter 1.</font></h1>```

Using CSS, the same element can be coded using style properties instead of HTML presentational 
attributes:

Chapter 1.\\n"}}">

```<h1 style="color: red;">Chapter 1.</h1>```

The advantages of this may not be immediately clear but the power of CSS becomes
more apparent when the style properties are placed in an internal style element or,
even better, an external CSS file. For example, suppose the document contains the
style element:

\\n    h1 {\\n        color: red;\\n    }\\n\\n"}}">

```<style>    h1 {        color: red;    }</style>```

All `h1` elements in the document will then automatically become red without requiring 
any explicit code. If the author later wanted to make `h1` elements blue instead, this 
could be done by changing the style element to:

\\n    h1 {\\n        color: blue;\\n    }\\n\\n"}}">

```<style>    h1 {        color: blue;    }</style>```

rather than by laboriously going through the document and changing the color for
each individual `h1` element.

The styles can also be placed in an external CSS file, as described below, and loaded
using syntax similar to:

\\n"}}">

```<link href="path/to/file.css" rel="stylesheet" type="text/css">```

This further decouples the styling from the HTML document and makes it possible to 
restyle multiple documents by simply editing a shared external CSS file.


### Sources
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
CSS, or Cascading Style Sheets, offers a flexible way to style web content, with 
styles originating from browser defaults, user preferences, or web designers. These 
styles can be applied inline, within an HTML document, or through external .css files 
for broader consistency. Not only does this simplify web development by promoting 
reusability and maintainability, it also improves site performance because styles 
can be offloaded into dedicated .css files that browsers can cache. Additionally, 
even if the styles cannot be loaded or are disabled, this separation maintains the 
accessibility and readability of the content, ensuring that the site is usable for 
all users, including those with disabilities. Its multi-faceted approach, including 
considerations for selector specificity, rule order, and media types, ensures that 
websites are visually coherent and adaptive across different devices and user needs, 
striking a balance between design intent and user accessibility.


#### Multiple style sheets
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
Multiple style sheets can be imported. Different styles can be applied depending 
on the output device being used; for example, the screen version can be quite different 
from the printed version, so authors can tailor the presentation appropriately for 
each medium.


#### Cascading
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
The style sheet with the highest priority controls the content display. Declarations 
not set in the highest priority source are passed on to a source of lower priority, 
such as the user agent style. The process is called *cascading*.

One of the goals of CSS is to allow users greater [control over presentation](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("). Someone who finds red italic headings difficult to read may apply a different style sheet. Depending on the browser and the website, a user may choose from various style sheets provided by the designers, or may remove all added styles, and view the site using the browser's default styling, or may override just the red italic heading style without altering other attributes. Browser extensions like [Stylish](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") and [Stylus](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") have been created to facilitate the management of such user style sheets. In the case of large projects, cascading can be used to determine which style has a higher priority when developers do integrate third-party styles that have conflicting priorities, and to further resolve those conflicts. Additionally, cascading can help create themed designs, which help designers fine-tune aspects of a design without compromising the overall layout.


##### CSS priority scheme
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")]
| CSS priority scheme (highest to lowest) |
|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| -                                       | -                                        | -                                                                                            |
| 1                                       | Importance                               | The "`!important`" annotation overwrites the previous priority types                         |
| 2                                       | Inline                                   | A style applied to an HTML element via HTML "style" attribute                                |
| 3                                       | Media Type                               | A property definition applies to all media types unless a media-specific CSS is defined      |
| 4                                       | User defined                             | Most browsers have the accessibility feature: a user-defined CSS                             |
| 5                                       | Selector specificity                     | A specific contextual selector (`#heading p`) overwrites generic definition                  |
| 6                                       | Rule order                               | Last rule declaration has a higher priority                                                  |
| 7                                       | Parent inheritance                       | If a property is not specified, it is inherited from a parent element                        |
| 8                                       | CSS property definition in HTML document | CSS rule or CSS inline style overwrites a default browser value                              |
| 9                                       | Browser default                          | The lowest priority: browser default value is determined by W3C initial value specifications |


### Specificity
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "background")]
*Specificity* refers to the relative weights of various rules.[[18]](mw:File/Thumb "background") 
It determines which styles apply to an element when more than one rule could apply. 
 Based on the specification, a simple selector (e.g. H1) has a specificity of 1, 
class selectors have a specificity of 1,0, and ID selectors have a specificity of 
1,0,0. Because the specificity values do not carry over as in the decimal system, 
commas are used to separate the "digits"[[19]](mw:File/Thumb "background") (a CSS 
rule having 11 elements and 11 classes would have a specificity of 11,11, not 121).

Thus the selectors of the following rule result in the indicated specificity:

| Selectors                           | Specificity |
|-------------------------------------|-------------|
| `h1 {color: white;}`                | 0, 0, 0, 1  |
| `p em {color: green;}`              | 0, 0, 0, 2  |
| `.grape {color: red;}`              | 0, 0, 1, 0  |
| `p.bright {color: blue;}`           | 0, 0, 1, 1  |
| `p.bright em.dark {color: yellow;}` | 0, 0, 2, 2  |
| `#id218 {color: brown;}`            | 0, 1, 0, 0  |
| `style=" "`                         | 1, 0, 0, 0  |


#### Examples
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "background")]
Consider this HTML fragment:

\\n\\n    \\n        \\n        \\n    \\n    \\n        
To demonstrate specificity\\n    \\n\\n"}}">

```<!DOCTYPE html><html>    <head>        <meta charset="utf-8">
<style>            #xyz { color: blue; }        </style>    </head>
<body>        <p id="xyz" style="color: green;">To demonstrate specificity</p>
</body></html>```

In the above example, the declaration in the `style` attribute overrides the one in the
`<style>` element because it has a higher specificity, and thus, the paragraph appears green:


To demonstrate specificity


### Inheritance
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "background")]
Inheritance is a key feature in CSS; it relies on the ancestor-descendant relationship
to operate. Inheritance is the mechanism by which properties are applied not only
to a specified element but also to its descendants.[[18]](mw:File/Thumb "button")
Inheritance relies on the document tree, which is the hierarchy of [XHTML](mw:File/Thumb "button") elements in a page based on nesting. Descendant elements may inherit CSS property values from any ancestor element enclosing them.In general, descendant elements inherit text-related properties, but their box-related properties are not inherited. Properties that can be inherited are color, font, letter spacing, line-height, list-style, text-align, text-indent, text-transform, visibility, white-space, and word-spacing. Properties that cannot be inherited are background, border, display, float and clear, height, and width, margin, min- and max-height and -width, outline, overflow, padding, position, text-decoration, vertical-align, and z-index.

Inheritance can be used to avoid declaring certain properties over and over again
in a style sheet, allowing for shorter CSS.

Inheritance in CSS is not the same as [inheritance in class-based programming languages](mw:File/Thumb "button"), where it is possible to define class B as "like class A, but with
modifications".[[20]](mw:File/Thumb "button") With CSS, it is possible to style
an *element* with "class A, but with modifications". However, it is not possible
to define a CSS *class* B like that, which could then be used to style multiple elements
without having to repeat the modifications.


#### Example
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Given the following style sheet:

```p {   color: blue;}```

Suppose there is a p element with an emphasizing element (`<em>`) inside:

\\n   This is to *illustrate inheritance\\n\\n"}}">

```<p>   This is to <em>illustrate</em> inheritance</p>```

If no color is assigned to the em element, the emphasized word "illustrate" inherits
the color of the parent element, p. The style sheet p has the color blue, hence,
the em element is likewise blue:


This is to *illustrate* inheritance


### Whitespace
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
The whitespace between properties and selectors is ignored. This code snippet:

```body{overflow:hidden;background:#000000;background-image:url(images/bg.gif);background-repeat:no-repeat;background-position:left 
top;}```

is functionally equivalent to this one:

```body {   overflow: hidden;   background-color: #000000;   background-image: url(images/bg.gif);
background-repeat: no-repeat;   background-position: left top;}```


#### Indentation
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]

Main article: [Indentation style](mw:File/Thumb "button")
One common way to format CSS for readability is to indent each property and give
it its own line. In addition to formatting CSS for readability, shorthand properties
can be used to write out the code faster, which also gets processed more quickly
when being rendered:[[21]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

```body {   overflow: hidden;   background: #000 url(images/bg.gif) no-repeat left 
top;}```

Sometimes, multiple property values are indented onto their own line:

```@font-face {   font-family: 'Comic Sans';   font-size: 20px;   src: url('first.example.com'),
url('second.example.com'),        url('third.example.com'),       
url('fourth.example.com');}```


### Positioning
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
CSS 2.1 defines three positioning schemes:
Normal flow*Inline* items are laid out in the same way as the letters in words in
the text, one after the other across the available space until there is no more room,
then starting a new line below. *Block* items stack vertically, like paragraphs and
like the items in a bulleted list. Normal flow also includes the relative positioning
of block or inline items and run-in boxes.FloatsA floated item is taken out of the
normal flow and shifted to the left or right as far as possible in the space available.
Other content then flows alongside the floated item.Absolute positioningAn absolutely
positioned item has no place in, and no effect on, the normal flow of other items.
It occupies its assigned position in its container independently of other items.[[22]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### Position property
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
There are five possible values of the `position` property. If an item is positioned in any
way other than `static`, then the further properties `top`, `bottom`, `left`, and `right` are used to specify
offsets and positions.The element having position static is not affected by the  
`top`, `bottom`, `left` or  `right` properties.


##### Static
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
The default value places the item in the *normal flow*.


##### Relative
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
The item is placed in the *normal flow*, and then shifted or offset from that position.
Subsequent flow items are laid out as if the item had not been moved.


##### Absolute
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
Specifies *absolute positioning*. The element is positioned in relation to its nearest
non-static ancestor.


##### Fixed
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
The item is *absolutely positioned* in a fixed position on the screen even as the
rest of the document is scrolled[[22]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### Float and clear
[[edit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.pygments%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cjquery.tablesorter.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available
skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")]
The `float` property may have one of three values. *Absolutely* positioned or *fixed*
items cannot be floated. Other elements normally flow around floated items, unless
they are prevented from doing so by their `clear` property.
leftThe item *floats* to the left of the line that it would have appeared in; other
items may flow around its right side.rightThe item *floats* to the right of the line
that it would have appeared in; other items may flow around its left side.clearForces
the element to appear underneath ('clear') floated elements to the left (`clear:left`), right
(`clear:right`) or both sides (`clear:both`).[[22]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.pygments%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cjquery.tablesorter.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")[[23]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.pygments%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cjquery.tablesorter.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

Several other style sheet languages for the web were proposed around the same time,

being released in 1996. In particular, a proposal by [Bert Bos](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") was influential; he became co-author of CSS1, and is regarded as co-creator of

Style sheets have existed in one form or another since the beginnings of Standard
Generalized Markup Language ([SGML](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")) in the 1980s, and CSS was developed to provide style sheets for the
web.[[28]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
One requirement for a web style sheet language was for style sheets to come from
different sources on the web. Therefore, existing style sheet languages like [DSSSL](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") and [FOSI](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") were not suitable. CSS, on the other hand, let a document's style be influenced by multiple style sheets by way of "cascading"
styles.[[28]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

As HTML grew, it came to encompass a wider variety of stylistic capabilities to meet
the demands of [web developers](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("). This evolution gave the designer more control over site appearance, at the cost of more complex HTML. Variations in [web browser](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") implementations, such as [ViolaWWW](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") and [WorldWideWeb](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url("),[[29]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
made consistent site appearance difficult, and users had less control over how web
content was displayed. The browser/editor developed by Tim Berners-Lee had style
sheets that were hard-coded into the program. The style sheets could therefore not
be linked to documents on the web.[[25]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
[Robert Cailliau](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("), also of CERN, wanted to separate the structure from the presentation so that different style sheets could describe different presentation for printing, screen-based presentations, and
editors.[[29]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

Improving web presentation capabilities was a topic of interest to many in the web
community and nine different style sheet languages were proposed on the www-style
mailing list.[[28]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Of these nine proposals, two were especially influential on what became CSS: Cascading
HTML Style Sheets[[24]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
and Stream-based Style Sheet Proposal (SSP).[[27]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")[[30]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Two browsers served as testbeds for the initial proposals; Lie worked with [Yves Lafon](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") to implement CSS in [Dave Raggett](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")'s [Arena](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
browser.[[31]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")[[32]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5)
url(")[[33]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Bert Bos implemented his own SSP proposal in the [Argo](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
browser.[[27]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Thereafter, Lie and Bos worked together to develop the CSS standard (the 'H' was
removed from the name because these style sheets could also be applied to other markup
languages besides HTML).[[25]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

Lie's proposal was presented at the "[Mosaic and the Web](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")" conference (later called WWW2) in Chicago, Illinois in 1994, and again with Bert Bos in
1995.[[25]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
Around this time the W3C was already being established and took an interest in the
development of CSS. It organized a workshop toward that end chaired by [Steven Pemberton](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("). This resulted in W3C adding work on CSS to the deliverables of the HTML editorial review board (ERB). Lie and Bos were the primary technical staff on this aspect of the project, with additional members, including [Thomas Reardon](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") of Microsoft, participating as well. In August 1996, [Netscape](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") Communication Corporation presented an alternative style sheet language called [JavaScript Style Sheets](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
(JSSS).[[25]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
The spec was never finished, and is deprecated.[[34]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")
By the end of 1996, CSS was ready to become official, and the CSS level 1 Recommendation
was published in December.

Development of HTML, CSS, and the [DOM](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") had all been taking place in one group, the HTML Editorial Review Board (ERB). Early in 1997, the ERB was split into three working groups: [HTML Working Group](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("), chaired by [Dan Connolly](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") of W3C; DOM Working group, chaired by Lauren Wood of [SoftQuad](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("); and [CSS Working Group](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url("), chaired by [Chris Lilley](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(") of W3C.

The CSS Working Group began tackling issues that had not been addressed with CSS
level 1, resulting in the creation of CSS level 2 on November 4, 1997. It was published
as a W3C Recommendation on May 12, 1998. CSS level 3, which was started in 1998,
is still under development as of 2014[[update]](mw:File/Thumb ") center no-repeat;display:block;margin:auto;width:50px;height:50px;border-radius:50%;position:absolute;left:50%;top:50%;transform:translate(-50%,-50%);transition:transform 120ms ease-out,background-color 120ms ease-out}.mw-tmh-player.audio .mw-tmh-play .mw-tmh-play-icon{background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5) url(")

In 2005, the CSS Working Groups decided to enforce the requirements for standards
more strictly. This meant that already published standards like CSS 2.1, CSS 3
Selectors, and CSS 3 Text were pulled back from Candidate Recommendation to Working
Draft level.


### Difficulty with adoption
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "background")]
The CSS 1 specification was completed in 1996. Microsoft's [Internet Explorer 3](mw:File/Thumb
"background")[[25]](mw:File/Thumb "background") was released that year, featuring
some limited support for CSS.  [IE 4](mw:File/Thumb "background") and [Netscape 4.x](mw:File/Thumb "background") added more support, but it was typically incomplete and had many [bugs](mw:File/Thumb "background") that prevented CSS from being usefully adopted. It was more than three years before any web browser achieved near-full implementation of the specification. [Internet Explorer 5.0](mw:File/Thumb "background") for the [Macintosh](mw:File/Thumb "background"), shipped in March 2000, was the first browser to have full (better than 99 percent)
CSS 1 support,[[35]](mw:File/Thumb "background") surpassing [Opera](mw:File/Thumb "background"), which had been the leader since its introduction of CSS support fifteen months earlier. Other browsers followed soon afterward, and many of them additionally implemented parts of
CSS 2.

However, even when later "version 5" web browsers began to offer a fairly full implementation
of CSS, they were still incorrect in certain areas. They were fraught with inconsistencies,
bugs, and other [quirks](mw:File/Thumb "background"). [Microsoft Internet Explorer 5. x for Windows](mw:File/Thumb "background"), as opposed to the very different [IE for Macintosh](mw:File/Thumb "background"), had a flawed implementation of the [CSS box model](mw:File/Thumb "background"), as compared with the CSS standards. Such inconsistencies and variation in feature support made it difficult for designers to achieve a consistent appearance across browsers and [platforms](mw:File/Thumb "background") without the use of [workarounds](mw:File/Thumb "background") termed [CSS hacks](mw:File/Thumb "background") and filters. The IE Windows box model bugs were so serious that, when [Internet Explorer 6](mw:File/Thumb "background") was released, Microsoft introduced a backward-compatible mode of CSS interpretation ("[quirks mode](mw:File/Thumb "background")") alongside an alternative, corrected "standards mode". Other non-Microsoft browsers also provided mode-switch capabilities. It, therefore, became necessary for authors of [HTML](mw:File/Thumb "background") files to ensure they contained special distinctive ["standards-compliant CSS intended" marker](mw:File/Thumb "background") to show that the authors intended CSS to be interpreted correctly, in compliance with standards, as opposed to being intended for the now long-obsolete [IE5/Windows browser](mw:File/Thumb "background"). Without this marker, web browsers with the "quirks mode"-switching capability will size objects in web pages as IE 5 on Windows would, rather than following CSS standards.

Problems with the patchy adoption of CSS and errata in the original specification
led the W3C to revise the CSS 2 standards into CSS 2.1, which moved nearer to a
working snapshot of current CSS support in HTML browsers. Some CSS 2 properties
that no browser successfully implemented were dropped, and in a few cases, defined
behaviors were changed to bring the standard into line with the predominant existing
implementations. CSS 2.1 became a Candidate Recommendation on February 25, 2004,
but CSS 2.1 was pulled back to Working Draft status on June 13, 2005,[[36]](mw:File/Thumb "background")
and only returned to Candidate Recommendation status on July 19, 2007.[[37]](mw:File/Thumb "background")

In addition to these problems, the `.css` extension was used by a software product used
to convert [PowerPoint](mw:File/Thumb "background") files into Compact Slide Show files,[[38]](mw:File/Thumb
"background")so some web servers served all `.css`[[39]](mw:File/Thumb "background")
as [MIME type](mw:File/Thumb "background") `application/x-pointplus`[[40]](mw:File/Thumb "background") rather
than `text/css`.


### Vendor prefixes
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "background")]
Individual browser vendors occasionally introduced new parameters ahead of standardization
and universalization. To prevent interfering with future implementations, vendors
prepended unique names to the parameters, such as `-moz-` for [Mozilla Firefox](mw:File/Thumb "background"), `-webkit-`
named after [the browsing engine](mw:File/Thumb "background") of [Apple Safari](mw:File/Thumb "background"), `-o-`
for [Opera Browser](mw:File/Thumb "background") and `-ms-` for [Microsoft Internet Explorer](mw:File/Thumb "background") and early versions of [Microsoft Edge](mw:File/Thumb "background") that use EdgeHTML.

Occasionally, the parameters with vendor prefixes such as `-moz-radial-gradient` and `-webkit-linear-gradient` have slightly
different syntax as compared to their non-vendor-prefix counterparts.[[41]](mw:File/Thumb "background")

Prefixed properties are rendered obsolete by the time of standardization. Programs
are available to automatically add prefixes for older browsers and to point out standardized
versions of prefixed parameters. Since prefixes are limited to a small subset of
browsers, removing the prefix allows other browsers to see the functionality. An
exception is certain obsolete `-webkit-` prefixed properties, which are so common and persistent
on the web that other families of browsers have decided to support them for compatibility.[[42]](mw:File/Thumb "background")
[![application/x-wiki](mw:ExtLink "background")](mw:File/Thumb "background")
CSS Snapshot 2021
CSS has various levels and profiles. Each level of CSS builds upon the last, typically
adding new features and typically denoted[[43]](mw:File/Thumb "background")  as CSS 1,
CSS 2, CSS 3, and CSS 4. Profiles are typically a subset of one or more levels
of CSS built for a particular device or user interface. Currently, there are profiles
for mobile devices, printers, and television sets. Profiles should not be confused
with media types, which were added in CSS 2.


#### CSS 1[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
The first  CSS specification to become an official W3C Recommendation is CSS level
1, published on 17 December 1996.  [Håkon Wium Lie](mw:File/Thumb "button") and [Bert Bos](mw:File/Thumb "button") are credited as the original
developers.[[44]](mw:File/Thumb "button")[[45]](mw:File/Thumb "button") Among its
capabilities are support for

- [Font](mw:File/Thumb "button") properties such as typeface and emphasis
- Color of text, backgrounds, and other elements
- Text attributes such as spacing between words, letters, and lines of text
- [Alignment](mw:File/Thumb "button") of text, images, [tables](mw:File/Thumb "button") and other elements
- Margin, border, padding, and positioning for most elements
- Unique identification and generic classification of groups of attributes

The W3C no longer maintains the CSS 1 Recommendation.[[46]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### CSS 2[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
CSS level 2 specification was developed by the W3C and published as a recommendation
in May 1998. A superset of CSS 1, CSS 2 includes a number of new capabilities like
absolute, relative, and fixed positioning of elements and [z-index](mw:File/Thumb "button"), the concept of media types, support for aural style sheets (which were later replaced by the CSS 3 speech
modules)[[47]](mw:File/Thumb "button") and bidirectional text, and new font properties
such as shadows.

The W3C no longer maintains the CSS 2 recommendation.[[48]](mw:File/Thumb "button")


#### CSS 2.1
[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]
CSS level 2 revision 1, often referred to as "CSS 2.1", fixes errors in CSS 2, removes
poorly supported or not fully interoperable features and adds already implemented
browser extensions to the specification. To comply with the W3C Process for standardizing
technical specifications, CSS 2.1 went back and forth between Working Draft status
and Candidate Recommendation status for many years. CSS 2.1 first became a [Candidate Recommendation](mw:File/Thumb "button") on 25 February 2004, but it was reverted to a Working Draft on 13 June 2005 for further review. It returned to Candidate Recommendation on 19 July 2007 and then updated twice in 2009. However, because changes and clarifications were made, it again went back to Last Call Working Draft on 7 December 2010.

CSS 2.1 went to Proposed Recommendation on 12 April 2011.[[49]](mw:File/Thumb "button")
After being reviewed by the W3C Advisory Committee, it was finally published as a
W3C Recommendation on 7 June 2011.[[50]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

CSS 2.1 was planned as the first and final revision of level 2—but low-priority
work on CSS 2.2 began in 2015.


#### CSS 3[[edit](mw:File/Thumb "button")]

"CSS3" redirects here. For other uses, see [CSS3 (disambiguation)](mw:File/Thumb "button").
Unlike CSS 2, which is a large single specification defining various features, CSS 3
is divided into several separate documents called "modules". Each module adds new
capabilities or extends features defined in CSS 2, preserving backward compatibility.
Work on CSS level 3 started around the time of publication of the original CSS 2
recommendation. The earliest CSS 3 drafts were published in June 1999.[[51]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

Due to the modularization, different modules have different stability and statuses.[[52]](mw:File/Thumb "button")

Some modules have *[Candidate Recommendation](mw:File/Thumb "button")* (*CR*) status
and are considered moderately stable. At *CR* stage, implementations are advised
to drop vendor prefixes.[[53]](mw:File/Thumb "button")
